summary.text: The ideal gas law relates the pressure, volume, temperature and amount of a gas through the equation PV = nRT, where R is the ideal gas constant.
The temperature in the equation must be absolute, measured in kelvins, where 0 K is −273.15 °C.
It applies only to an ideal gas or as an approximation to real gases, and is most accurate for monatomic gases at high temperatures and low pressures.

facts.label: Kinetic derivation
facts.value: August Krönig in 1856 and Rudolf Clausius in 1857, independently

facts.label: Most accurate for
facts.value: Monatomic gases at high temperatures and low pressures

items.prompt: A thermometer reads 25 °C. How should the temperature enter the ideal gas equation?

options.label: As 25, exactly as it is
Shifted to the Kelvin scale first
As 0, since 25 °C is mild
As −273.15 plus nothing else

items.explain: The equation needs an absolute temperature, in kelvins; the Kelvin scale is a shifted Celsius scale.

items.prompt: Which sample of gas would follow the ideal gas law most closely?

options.label: A noble gas that is cold and squeezed
A diatomic gas that is cold and squeezed
A diatomic gas that is cold and thinly spread
A noble gas that is hot and under low pressure

items.explain: The law is most accurate for monatomic gases at high temperatures and low pressures, and noble gases are monatomic.

items.prompt: Why does the law fit better when a gas is spread into a larger volume at lower pressure?

options.label: Neighbouring molecules end up far apart compared with their size
Molecules grow smaller as the pressure drops
Molecules begin to attract each other strongly
Molecules stop moving and lose their energy

items.explain: At lower densities the distance between adjacent molecules becomes much larger than the molecular size, so size matters less.

items.prompt: Why does heating a gas make the law work better?

options.label: Molecules become larger and fill the container
Molecules lose all motion at higher temperature
Attractions between molecules matter less as their energy rises
Heat adds new kinds of attraction between molecules

items.explain: The relative importance of intermolecular attractions diminishes with increasing thermal kinetic energy, so with increasing temperature.

items.prompt: A real gas expands freely into a larger space and its temperature changes. What explains this?

options.label: Its molecules vanish as it expands
Its temperature stays fixed for every real gas
Its molecules are far larger than an ideal gas's
Its molecules attract or repel one another, which an ideal gas ignores

items.explain: For an ideal gas free expansion leaves the temperature constant, but real gas molecules interact, so heating or cooling occurs (the Joule–Thomson effect).

items.prompt: If gas molecules do not attract each other, what kind of energy does the gas hold?

options.label: All of its energy is motion energy of its molecules
Mostly energy stored in attractions between molecules
Half motion energy and half stored energy
No energy of any kind

items.explain: With no intermolecular attractions, potential energy is zero, so all the energy is the kinetic energy of the molecules.
